🚨 9/11: THE SECOND WAVE — CAN WE ACTUALLY MEASURE IT?

For months, many of us have noticed something happening online: people are questioning the official 9/11 narrative again—and the conversation appears substantially larger than it was just five years ago.

But rather than relying on anecdotal observations, I wanted to see whether we could actually quantify it.

So we created a 9/11 Alternative-Narrative Digital Attention Index, using the 20th anniversary in 2021 as our baseline of 100 and comparing it with each year through the 25th anniversary in 2026.

The index looks at several signals: comparable engagement with 9/11-questioning content, the reach of major videos/posts and podcasts, search interest, and available public-opinion polling. Because historical data from X, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook aren’t uniformly available, this is a directional composite index—not a literal count of every 9/11 post or impression on the Internet.

And that’s an important distinction.

📊 THE RESULT:

2021 — 100
2022 — 134
2023 — 169
2024 — 342
2025 — 409
2026 — 714

In other words, our preliminary index puts today’s digital attention surrounding alternative 9/11 narratives at roughly 7X the 2021 baseline.

And there are hard numbers underneath that trend.

🔹 A comparable Reddit/Building 7 engagement measure rose from roughly 750 interactions in 2021 to more than 6,000 in 2026.

🔹 In 2023, the viral “Letter to America” episode generated roughly 13.7 MILLION TikTok views, demonstrating how quickly a new generation could suddenly encounter 9/11-related material.

🔹 In 2024, resurfaced 9/11 footage reportedly generated 60+ MILLION views on X.

🔹 By 2025, individual long-form programs questioning aspects of 9/11 were routinely generating 1–3 MILLION+ views, as major personalities brought Building 7, intelligence failures, alleged foreknowledge and other questions to enormous audiences.

🔹 And in 2026, an Emerson national poll found 25% of Americans saying they believe the U.S. government helped plan the attacks. That measures belief—not merely clicks.

But perhaps the most interesting finding is WHEN the acceleration begins.

It wasn’t September 2026.

The curve starts bending sharply upward around 2023–2024, accelerates again in 2025, and then explodes into the 25th anniversary.

That suggests the anniversary didn’t necessarily create this resurgence.

It amplified something already underway.

And there may be a simple reason.

Twenty years ago, if someone wanted to investigate Building 7 or alternative explanations for 9/11, they generally had to SEARCH for the information.

Today the information searches for YOU.

TikTok. X. Instagram Reels. YouTube Shorts. Podcasts.

Someone can encounter a 30-second Building 7 clip without ever searching “9/11 Truth.” The algorithm serves another clip, then an interview, archival footage, a podcast—and suddenly someone born years after September 11 is examining questions that were once largely confined to specialized websites and documentaries.

That’s the fundamental transformation we’re trying to measure:

9/11 skepticism has moved from a largely SEARCH-LED subculture toward FEED-LED mass distribution.

And that’s why I think we’re witnessing something much larger than another anniversary news cycle.

2021: Persistence.
2023: Rediscovery.
2024: Viral breakout.
2025: Mainstream alternative-media breakthrough.
2026: Convergence.

Twenty-five years later, a new generation isn’t simply remembering September 11.

They’re discovering it—and asking questions of their own.
